personality_voice.book_baseline: Across all seven books, Snape's voice is one of the most precisely defined in the series: cold, measured, weaponized restraint. He speaks in controlled, deliberate sentences — long rhetorical constructions, strategic pauses, sardonic repetition, mock politeness deployed as contempt. He rarely shouts; his menace is delivered quietly. His physical register (swooping cloak, cold eyes, low voice, deliberate pace) is inseparable from his personality. When he does erupt — the Shrieking Shack, the Pensieve expulsion in OotP, the 'Do not call me coward' flight — these breaks are notable precisely because they violate his iron control. The books accumulate this portrait across thousands of interactions: classroom sadism toward Neville, rhetorical humiliation of Harry, barely suppressed fury at Dumbledore's overrulings, and occasional sardonic wit ('Would you like me to compose an epitaph?'). The result is a voice that is instantly recognizable and deeply specific — not merely 'cold teacher' but a psychologically precise portrait of a man who has learned to weaponize restraint as a survival mechanism.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: Alan Rickman's performance preserves the surface architecture of Snape's voice with genuine fidelity across all eight films. The deliberate cadence, the cold precision, the sardonic register, and the theatrical menace are all present. Key moments land: 'Turn to page 394,' 'Obviously,' 'I may vomit,' 'Do not call me coward,' 'Always.' The impassivity under Voldemort's scrutiny, the composure at the Astronomy Tower, and the controlled delivery throughout the Prince's Tale are strong. However, the films systematically compress or eliminate the sustained, granular texture that gives the book voice its depth: the extended rhetorical performances across multiple classroom scenes, the accumulated petty cruelties toward Neville, the full emotional eruptions (the hospital wing meltdown in PoA, the thrown jar in OotP), and the richest extended displays of his intelligence (the Spinner's End interrogation in HBP, the Marauder's Map staircase in GoF). The films deliver his personality in set-pieces rather than through the accumulated, daily behavioural pattern of the books.
personality_voice.difference: The films preserve the dominant register — cold contempt, controlled menace, sardonic precision — reliably enough that Snape is always recognizable as Snape. What is systematically lost is the texture: the sustained classroom sadism that builds him as a systematic abuser of institutional power rather than an episodic antagonist; the specific eruption moments that reveal the depth of his wounds; the long rhetorical performances (Spinner's End above all) that demonstrate his intelligence and emotional discipline at full stretch. The emotional mechanics of his personality — the controlled surface hiding catastrophic wounds — are legible in the films but thinner than in the books. Across seven books, the films deliver perhaps 70% of the personality surface and 50% of the depth.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings, with consistent findings: surface traits preserved, textural depth and sustained behavioural pattern compressed in every installment.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The per-book scores range from 16 (OotP) to 21 (CoS, DH). The highest scores are in books where Snape's personality is relatively contained and the films capture the key scenes (CoS, DH Prince's Tale). The lowest is OotP, where the specific texture of his voice — the weaponized quiet, the rhetorical construction, the eruption after the Pensieve — is most compressed. The synthesis weighted toward the most characterologically important books (OotP, HBP, DH) where the personality texture is most complex and the film compression most damaging. The consistent pattern across all books — surface preserved, depth compressed — warrants a score of 18: recognizable and credible, but with meaningful, systematic reduction of the textural density that makes the character distinctively himself.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Across the series, Snape serves as one of the most structurally active characters: a sustained red herring (PS through HBP), an active investigator and obstacle (PS, CoS, PoA, GoF), an Order operative performing real intelligence work (OotP, HBP, DH), the agent of Dumbledore's death (HBP), a covert protector executing a long-term plan (OotP through DH), and finally the posthumous narrative engine whose memories resolve the central mystery of the series (DH). His agency is not decorative — he consistently initiates, decides, and changes events. The most consequential single act of agency in the series (outside Voldemort) is arguably Snape's: delivering the prophecy fragment, then spending two decades as a double agent to atone for it.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films preserve Snape's structural functions in outline: the red herring (PS, CoS), the Occlumency teacher (OotP, compressed), the Unbreakable Vow and killing of Dumbledore (HBP), the Prince's Tale revelation (DH). However, across every book adaptation, specific acts of active agency are removed: the Dark Mark confrontation with Fudge and the spy mission (GoF); the Order-alerting sequence after Harry's coded message (OotP); the Mundungus Confunding decoy plan (DH); the Spinner's End interrogation as active management of Bellatrix (HBP, compressed); the Marauder's Map staircase deduction (GoF); the sustained protective interventions as Headmaster (DH). The pattern is consistent: the films retain Snape's structural narrative position but remove the active, initiating dimension of his agency in favour of reactive or functional presence.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The most damaging single agency loss across the series is the GoF spy mission (Snape returning to Voldemort on Dumbledore's orders), which defines his character for the remainder of the series and is entirely absent from the film. The second most damaging is the OotP Order-alerting sequence, which demonstrates Snape as a functioning double agent doing real consequential work. The DH Mundungus decoy is the third significant loss. In each case, the omission is not compensated by transfer to another character — the action simply disappears. The films' Snape is structurally present but operationally passive compared to the books.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all seven per-book scorings. The absent material is confirmed in the book corpus; the film corpus does not contain it.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Per-book scores range from 13 (OotP, GoF, HBP) to 16 (CoS, DH). The consistent midrange reflects a character whose structural role survives but whose active agency is repeatedly pruned. The synthesis weighted GoF and DH most heavily for this dimension: GoF because the spy mission omission is the single most consequential agency loss in the series, and DH because the Mundungus decoy and the sustained headmaster-year agency together represent a significant reduction in active protective function. A score of 13 reflects a character whose narrative position is legible but whose agency is clearly and systematically altered.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: The books construct Snape's motivations across seven volumes into one of the most layered character portraits in children's literature. The foundation is Lily: not simple romantic longing but a foundational organizing principle — she is the reason he betrayed Voldemort, the reason he agreed to spy, the reason he accepted Dumbledore's most terrible instruction, and the reason he protected a child he could not bring himself to like. Layered over this: guilt (over the prophecy, over the 'Mudblood' incident); wounded pride and resentment (toward Harry as James-by-proxy, toward Dumbledore for using him); self-preservation and cold calculation; constrained loyalty to Dumbledore that coexists with genuine resentment of his manipulation; and a professional pride in dangerous competence that the books show through the 'satisfied' expression when Harry names his job. The internal conflict — between hatred of Harry and obligation to protect him, between duty to Dumbledore and resentment of that duty, between his Slytherin formation and his hidden loyalty — is never resolved in the books; it is the engine of his characterisation.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films preserve the Lily motivation clearly, especially in DH's Prince's Tale, and the 'Always' moment distils the durability of his love effectively. The guilt dimension is present in the 'pig for slaughter' shock (DH) and the Patronus scene. The resentment of Dumbledore is present but softened — the films compress the combative exchanges and reduce the 'You have used me' dimension. The distinction between protecting Harry and caring for Harry is preserved in the Patronus structure. However, the specific psychological texture is repeatedly flattened: the 'satisfied' spy pride (OotP) is absent; the convulsive forearm grip signalling Dark Mark anxiety (GoF) is absent; the sustained internal conflict between pedagogical duty and personal hatred during Occlumency (OotP) is compressed; the Trelawney backstory connecting the prophecy to Lily's death (HBP) is absent from the film. The film's motivational picture is 'Snape loved Lily and protected Harry because of it' — which is correct but is a substantial simplification of the books' 'Snape loved Lily, is tormented by guilt over her death, protects Harry from obligation not affection, resents both Harry and Dumbledore, and is capable of sustained petty cruelty toward the very child he is risking his life to protect.'
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The primary motivation (Lily) is preserved. The secondary motivations — pride, resentment, guilt, self-preservation — are present in reduced form. The internal conflict — the coexistence of genuine hatred and genuine obligation, the tension between past and present self — is legible but flattened. The film removes or compresses the specific signals that make the internal conflict textured: the forearm grip, the 'satisfied' expression, the 'You've used me' confrontations at full intensity, the Trelawney revelation that gives his guilt its specific object. The motivation survives as a fact (he loved Lily, he protected Harry) without the full psychological architecture that gives it its moral weight.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all per-book scorings. The absent material is confirmed in the book corpus.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Per-book scores consistently cluster at 9-11 with DH reaching 13 (where the Lily motivation is most fully preserved). The synthesis reflects this pattern: the primary motivation is present throughout, but the psychological complexity — the specific guilt, the resentment, the internal conflict between hatred and duty — is repeatedly compressed. A score of 10 reflects motivations that are partially flattened or underexplained: directionally correct, missing the architecture that makes them morally uncomfortable rather than simply tragic.

character_arc.book_baseline: Snape's series arc is one of the most carefully constructed in the books: from apparent villain (PS), through sustained ambiguity maintained across six volumes under deliberate reader misdirection, to the posthumous revelation in DH that reframes his entire presence retroactively. The arc's key structural beats are: PS (reluctant protector from impure motives, enmity unchanged); PoA (schoolboy grudge overrides professional duty); GoF (former Death Eater re-enters spy role at great personal risk — the arc's hinge); OotP (Occlumency failure shows his wound overriding his mission); HBP (kills Dumbledore as agreed, maintaining cover at terrible cost); DH (dies maintaining the performance to the end, vindicated posthumously). Each book contributes a specific arc beat. The arc is not one of transformation — Snape does not become a better person — but of revelation: we learn that the cruelty and the hidden goodness coexisted all along, and that the goodness was both real and insufficient to make him a good man.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The films preserve the arc's beginning (PS as red herring and reluctant protector), certain middle elements (PoA grudge, HBP killing), and the end (DH Prince's Tale and death). The structural shape — apparent villain to posthumously vindicated double agent — is legible. However, the arc's most important hinge (GoF spy mission) is entirely absent, meaning the transition from 'suspected villain' to 'confirmed double agent re-entering mortal danger' is never dramatised. The OotP micro-arc (wound overriding mission) is compressed to the point where its consequence — that Snape's personal failure contributed to Sirius's death — is not conveyed. The HBP arc intermediate steps (DADA teaching, Trelawney revelation, full Half-Blood Prince backstory) are missing, accelerating the arc's trajectory through its most complex section. The DH headmaster-year arc — Snape as covert protector exercising constrained agency under Voldemort's occupation — is largely absent from the film.
character_arc.difference: The arc's frame (beginning and end) is preserved. The arc's most important individual beats within the middle volumes are systematically compressed or absent. The GoF hinge is the single most damaging loss: without it, the audience never sees the moment when Snape voluntarily re-enters mortal danger, which is the proof of his commitment and the foundation of everything that follows. The OotP consequence (Snape's failure contributing to a death) is absent, which means the arc has no failure beat — it moves from competent spy to tragic hero without the intermediate moment of genuine culpable failure. The DH arc is somewhat romanticised through the Prince's Tale frame, which positions Snape primarily as tragic lover rather than as the contradictory, occasionally monstrous figure the books maintain to the end.
character_arc.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all per-book scorings.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Per-book scores range from 9 (HBP, where the arc is most compressed) to 13 (PoA, CoS, where the arc is intentionally flat or structurally simple). The synthesis weighted GoF and HBP most heavily, as these are the arc's two most complex installments and both have significant compression. The GoF spy mission omission alone warrants significant reduction. A score of 10 reflects an arc that is compressed, missing its most important transitional beat (the spy mission), and romanticised at its conclusion — present in outline but missing the specific steps that give it its moral weight.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Snape's web of relationships across the series is unusually complex: Snape/Harry (mutual enmity containing concealed protection, coexisting with genuine reciprocal hatred — the series' central relational paradox); Snape/Lily (foundational, defining, unrequited, guilt-freighted); Snape/Dumbledore (asymmetric trust, obligation, manipulation, constrained loyalty with genuine resentment — the engine of the plot); Snape/James (historical, defining through its poison — the wound that shapes every other relationship); Snape/Voldemort (performance under mortal danger, total concealment of true loyalty); and key individual-book relationships: Snape/Sirius (mutual loathing, psychological warfare, OotP), Snape/Lupin (old near-death wound, PoA), Snape/Malfoy (protective but adversarial, HBP), Snape/Neville (predatory institutional power, every year). These relationships are active, bidirectional, and dramatically consequential.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Lily relationship is well served across films, particularly in DH. The Dumbledore relationship is preserved in structural outline but consistently softened — the resentment, the 'You have used me' confrontation, the combative exchanges are compressed across HBP and DH. The Voldemort relationship is well preserved in the boathouse scene and Malfoy Manor. The Snape/Harry relationship retains antagonism throughout but loses the sustained, textured dimension of simultaneous hatred and concealed protection — and, crucially, the post-Pensieve complexity in OotP and the headmaster-year dynamic in DH. The Snape/Sirius relationship (tactical psychological warfare, OotP) is reduced to surface hostility. The Snape/Lupin relationship loses the full backstory elaboration (PoA). The Snape/Neville relationship is almost entirely absent from the films — Neville names Snape as his greatest fear but the relationship that produces that fear is never shown. The Snape/Malfoy relationship is present but compressed (HBP).
key_relationships.difference: The films preserve the existence of Snape's key relationships but consistently reduce their emotional dynamics and power balances. The most damaging losses are: the Snape/Harry relationship losing its covert protection dimension and the complexity of the headmaster year; the Snape/Dumbledore relationship losing the resentment and combative dimension that makes it a genuine tension rather than simple loyalty; the Snape/Neville relationship being entirely absent (removing the most consistent evidence of his predatory institutional cruelty); the Snape/Sirius dynamic losing its tactical quality (OotP). The Lily relationship is the exception — it is well preserved in its essential structure.
key_relationships.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all per-book scorings.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Per-book scores range from 6 (OotP, GoF, HBP) to 8 (CoS). The consistent pattern is that key relationships are preserved in surface dynamic but reduced in emotional complexity and power balance. The synthesis applied score cap rule 2 (key relationships change substantially) to the Snape/Neville, Snape/Sirius, and Snape/Dumbledore-combative-dimension losses. The Lily relationship prevents a lower score. A score of 6 reflects relationships that are consistently recognizable but substantially reduced across the board, with the most important individual-book relationships (Sirius in OotP, Lupin in PoA, Dumbledore's combative dimension in HBP/DH) meaningfully altered or absent.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The books construct Snape as one of literature's most carefully designed morally complex characters: a man who is genuinely cruel (the Neville predation is not ambiguous, the 'I see no difference' comment is gratuitous, the petty vindictiveness is real) and simultaneously performing acts of genuine courage and loyalty at great personal cost. The complexity is not that he is secretly good — it is that the cruelty and the goodness coexist without resolution. Key layers: the simultaneous genuine cruelty and genuine protective function; the specific guilt over Lily (the prophecy, the 'Mudblood' incident) that drives everything without excusing anything; the pride in dangerous competence that is not mere ego; the wounded-child backstory (Pensieve, Spinner's End) that explains but does not excuse; the performance artist dimension (Spinner's End interrogation as the single greatest display of his intelligence); the resentment of Dumbledore that coexists with genuine loyalty; the specificity of his love for Lily as distinct from any warmth toward Harry; the habitual cruelty that makes the covert kindness meaningful by contrast.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The films retain the arc-essential nuances: the Lily motivation, the Prince's Tale revelation, the 'Always' moment, the Patronus distinction, the 'pig for slaughter' moral shock. They consistently lose the material that makes the complexity morally uncomfortable rather than romantically tragic: the sustained habitual cruelty toward Neville (absent across all films); the full Spinner's End interrogation (the single richest display of his intelligence, compressed to near-nothing in HBP); the Trelawney backstory connecting the prophecy to Lily's death (HBP, absent); the GoF spy mission that proves his courage (absent); the OotP Order actions that prove his competence as a double agent (absent); the full emotional collapses (hospital wing PoA, thrown jar OotP) that show his psychological fragility; the torn photograph detail (DH) that shows the specificity and limits of his love; the Yule Ball Karkaroff exchange where Dumbledore witnesses Snape's courage directly (DH, cut). The film's Snape is primarily encountered as a tragic-romantic figure in the Prince's Tale, which accurately captures his love for Lily but frames him more sympathetically than the books, which insist on maintaining the cruelty alongside the tragedy.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The most damaging systematic loss across the series is the absence of the sustained habitual cruelty that gives the covert kindness its meaning. In the books, Snape's complexity rests on the simultaneous coexistence of genuine ugliness and hidden goodness — neither cancels the other. The films, by compressing or eliminating the Neville predation, the petty classroom sadism, and the full emotional meltdowns, tip the balance toward a more conventionally tragic reading. The result is a character whose ambiguity is preserved as a plot function (Is he loyal? — yes) but whose moral complexity is reduced (the fact that he remains genuinely cruel even while being loyal is softened). The Spinner's End omission removes the series' single most sophisticated extended character scene. The Trelawney and GoF mission omissions remove two of the three most important complexity-establishing moments.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced across all per-book scorings. The absent material is confirmed in the book corpus.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Per-book scores range from 8 (OotP, GoF, HBP) to 11 (CoS, DH). The synthesis weighted HBP most heavily for this dimension — the Spinner's End compression is the single largest loss of nuance in the entire adaptation — and OotP second, where the full emotional collapse and the Order-action revelation are both absent. The consistent pattern across all books is a character whose broad complexity signal (ambiguous, not simply a villain) is preserved but whose specific, morally uncomfortable texture — the cruelty that coexists with the goodness — is systematically softened. A score of 8 reflects noticeable simplification: important nuances, the habitual cruelty dimension, the specific intelligence displays, and several defining character moments are missing, leaving a version of Snape that is complex in outline but considerably thinner in the material that makes that complexity genuinely uncomfortable.

comparative.key_observations: The films' Severus Snape earns a total of 65 out of 100 — a score that reflects a character who is tonally and structurally recognizable throughout, but who has been systematically reduced in the specific material that made him one of the most genuinely complex characters in the source texts. Alan Rickman's performance preserves the surface architecture of the character with considerable skill: the cold precision, the sardonic register, the composure under pressure, and the devastation of key emotional moments (the Prince's Tale, 'Always') are all creditable. The films fail Snape most severely in three interconnected dimensions. First, agency: the GoF spy mission, the OotP Order-alerting sequence, and the DH Mundungus decoy plan are the three most consequential active choices Snape makes in the series, and all three are absent from the films — leaving a character who occupies his structural position without being seen to do the work that position requires. Second, the complexity mechanism: the books' Snape is morally uncomfortable precisely because his genuine cruelty and his genuine covert goodness coexist without resolution; the films, by compressing the sustained Neville predation, the full emotional collapses, and the specific ugliness of his character, tip him toward a tragic-romantic frame that is simpler and more sympathetic than the books intend. Third, the HBP adaptation is the single most damaging individual installment — the Spinner's End interrogation, the DADA classroom arc, the Trelawney revelation, and the extended Snape/Harry antagonism are all absent, stripping the book that should have been Snape's most complex cinematic appearance down to its plot skeleton. The films deliver Snape's story but not his full character.
